structure.title: Sustainability statements
structure.heading: 2 Sustainability statements
structure.start_phrase: The sustainability statement s have been prepared on a consolidated basis .
structure.summary:
- Document section: UniCredit 2024 Annual Reports and Accounts – Consolidated report on operations, Sustainability statements, ESRS 2 General Information.
- Basis for preparation (BP-1): First sustainability statements prepared in compliance with ESRS, replacing the former GRI-based Integrated Report; prepared on a consolidated basis with the same perimeter as the financial statements (all line-by-line consolidated entities included).
- Perimeter details: Subsidiaries in scope are listed in the Notes (Part A – Accounting policies, Section 3). Controlled but not consolidated companies were assessed as not material for sustainability and are not included.
- Legal framework and exemptions: Under Italian Legislative Decree 125/2024 (art.7.1), several subsidiaries (UniCredit Bank DD, UniCredit Bulbank AD, UniCredit Bank Hungary Zrt, AO UniCredit Bank, UniCredit Bank Serbia Jsc, UniCredit Banka Slovenija DD) are exempt from preparing separate sustainability reports as they are covered by the parent’s consolidated statements.
- Entities preparing sub-consolidated reports: Due to size (>500 employees) and listed status, Zagrebacka Banka DD, UniCredit Bank Czech Republic and Slovakia AS, UniCredit Bank SA, UniCredit Bank Austria AG, and UniCredit Bank GmbH will publish their own sustainability reporting. Despite delayed local transposition of the EU Directive, UniCredit Bank Austria AG and UniCredit Bank GmbH will report for 2024 covering their full perimeter.
- Value chain coverage: Statements cover upstream (primarily tier 1 suppliers and business partners) and downstream (clients, investees, business partners) segments. Upstream focus includes responsible sourcing, environmental and social practices, and Scope 3 GHG emissions related to purchased goods and services (e.g., categories 1, 2, 7). Disclosures include quantitative Scope 3 metrics and qualitative information on material impacts, risks, opportunities, and related policies, actions, and targets (PATs).
- Completeness: No omission of relevant information such as intellectual property, know-how, or innovation outcomes.
- Disclosures in specific circumstances (BP-2): Time horizons defined as short term (<1 year), medium term (>1–5 years), and long term (5–10+ years). These are consistently applied across ESG strategy, risk management, and governance, aligned with financial reporting, industry standards, and strategic goals (e.g., net-zero by 2050) and transition plans in response to regulation.

- Context: UniCredit’s 2024 Consolidated report on operations – Sustainability statements, prepared under ESRS 2 (General information), focusing on Basis for Preparation (BP-1) and Disclosures in Specific Circumstances (BP-2).

- Consolidation perimeter mirrors the financial statements: all line-by-line consolidated entities are included; controlled but not consolidated companies were assessed as not material for sustainability and therefore excluded.
- Legal framework: per Italian Legislative Decree 125/2024, several subsidiaries are exempt from issuing their own sustainability reports as they are covered by UniCredit’s consolidated statements (e.g., UniCredit Bank DD, UniCredit Bulbank AD, UniCredit Bank Hungary Zrt, AO UniCredit Bank, UniCredit Bank Serbia Jsc, UniCredit Banka Slovenija DD).
- Subsidiaries required to publish sub-consolidated sustainability reports due to size (>500 employees) and listing status: Zagrebacka Banka DD, UniCredit Bank Czech Republic and Slovakia AS, UniCredit Bank SA, UniCredit Bank Austria AG, UniCredit Bank GmbH. Austria AG and GmbH chose to publish 2024 reports despite delayed national transposition of the EU directive.
- Value chain coverage: 
  - Upstream: mainly tier 1 suppliers and business partners; assessment of impacts, risks, and opportunities around responsible sourcing, environmental and social practices; includes Scope 3 GHG (notably categories 1, 2, 7) and actions to promote sustainable procurement.
  - Downstream: direct clients, investees, and business partners.
- Disclosures as of 31 Dec 2024 include quantitative Scope 3 GHG metrics and qualitative information on material impacts, risks and opportunities (IROs) and related policies, actions, and targets (PATs), with cross-references to SBM-3 and IRO-1.
- No omissions of relevant information, including intellectual property, know-how, or innovation outcomes.
- Time horizons defined for reporting and strategy: short term (<1 year), medium term (>1–5 years), long term (5–10+ years); applied consistently across ESG strategy, risk management, and governance; aligned with financial reporting, industry standards, and strategic goals such as net-zero by 2050 and regulatory transition plans.

nodes.title: Basis for preparation
nodes.heading: 2.1.1 Basis for preparation
nodes.start_phrase: The sustainability statement s have been prepared on a consolidated basis .
nodes.summary:
- Purpose and framework: First sustainability statements prepared under ESRS, replacing prior GRI-based Integrated Report; prepared on a consolidated basis with the same perimeter as the financial statements.
- Consolidation scope: All line-by-line consolidated entities are included; controlled but not consolidated companies assessed as non-material for sustainability and excluded. Subsidiaries in several CEE countries are exempt from standalone reporting as they are covered by the parent’s statements; certain large, listed subsidiaries will publish sub-consolidated sustainability reports. UniCredit Bank Austria AG and UniCredit Bank GmbH publish 2024 reports despite pending local transposition.
- Value chain coverage: Reporting covers both upstream (primarily tier 1 suppliers/business partners) and downstream (clients, investees, business partners) segments. Focus areas include responsible sourcing, environmental and social practices, and Scope 3 GHG emissions (including purchased goods/services and other relevant categories). Disclosures include quantitative Scope 3 data and qualitative material impacts, risks and opportunities (IROs) and related policies, actions and targets (PATs). No omissions for IP or innovation.
- Time horizons: Defined as short term (<1 year), medium term (>1–5 years), and long term (5–10+ years), aligned with strategy, risk management, financial reporting, stakeholder expectations, and TCFD.
- Data, estimation, and methodologies: For value chain metrics (notably Scope 3), primary data is used where available; otherwise, estimates are applied due to scale/complexity, limited sector-specific standards for financial institutions, tooling constraints, and counterparty data limitations. Mapping focuses on first-tier counterparties. Financed emissions estimated for non-financial corporates and households; financial institutions and government-related counterparties excluded in the first ESRS year. Methodologies follow the GHG Protocol and PCAF, using emissions factors, proxy data, and scenario analysis (baseline, delayed transition, energy disorder). Measurement uncertainty is acknowledged; assumptions and estimation methods are disclosed, data is controlled for accuracy, and aligned with financial statement assumptions. Ongoing engagement with clients/suppliers and external providers aims to improve data quality and methods over time.
- Reporting boundaries and references: Prior-period ESRS comparisons and error disclosures are not applicable before the first ESRS year. Additional legal disclosures are limited to EU Taxonomy Article 8. Certain climate-related risk identification processes (IRO-1) are incorporated by reference to the Notes, Part E.
- Governance structure (GOV-1): UniCredit adopts a one-tier model with a Board of Directors and an internal Audit Committee; complies with Italian and EU regulations, Bank of Italy rules, and obligations tied to listings in Milan, Frankfurt, and Warsaw. The Board has 14 members (1 executive CEO/General Manager; 13 non-executives). The Audit Committee comprises 4 independent non-executive directors; the chair is elected by minority shareholders. Additional committees: Governance & Sustainability (4 members), Risk (4), Nomination (3), Remuneration (3), and Related-Parties (3). The Board appoints the CEO to execute board resolutions. No employee representation is foreseen by law or bylaws. Directors are appointed via slate voting to ensure minority representation and gender balance. The Board defines an optimal qualitative/quantitative composition, publishes a theoretical profile before renewals, and discloses alignment outcomes; specific recommendations were provided ahead of the 2024–2026 renewal.

nodes.title: Governance
nodes.heading: 2.1.2 Governance
nodes.summary:
- Governance structure and composition: UniCredit’s Board of Directors comprises 14 members (1 executive CEO/General Manager and 13 non-executive). The Board is supported by six committees: Audit (4 independent members; chair elected by minorities), Governance & Sustainability, Risk, Nomination, Remuneration, and Related-Parties. Committee sizes: Governance & Sustainability and Risk (4 members each); Nomination, Remuneration, Related-Parties (3 each). Directors are elected via slate voting to ensure minority representation; no employee representation is foreseen.

- Board selection, capabilities, and training: The Board defines an optimal “theoretical profile” and required qualifications, including ESG and legal/compliance expertise, and ensures gender balance. A permanent three-year induction and training program is in place, including ESG-focused sessions (e.g., 2024 session on approach, regulation, Net Zero).

- Skills matrix and diversity: All core competencies identified in the theoretical profile are represented (international markets, banking governance/business, legal/compliance, strategy, risk/control, accounting/audit, ESG, digital/technology). The Board shows strong diversity and independence (e.g., 50% women; 93% independent; broad international experience). Committee compositions meet independence and expertise requirements, with detailed gender/age/geography breakdowns.

- Strategic oversight and risk governance: The Board sets overall strategy, including the Group’s ESG strategy and KPIs, and approves the Risk Appetite Framework (RAF), which includes climate risk KPIs. The Audit Committee assesses adequacy of financial and non-financial (ESG) reporting. The Risk Committee oversees risk strategy and policies, including climate and environmental risk. The Governance & Sustainability Committee advises on non-risk ESG matters. The CEO identifies risks, proposes strategy, ensures execution of RAF and policies, and maintains internal information flows. Roles reflect non-delegable supervisory and management responsibilities and align with ESRS double materiality.

- Management bodies and ESG integration: The Group Executive Committee (GEC), chaired by the CEO, sets ESG strategy, targets and acts as the Group’s risk council; it contributed to the 2024 double materiality assessment. Managerial committees include the Group Non-Financial Risks & Controls Committee (reputational/sensitive sectors, non-financial risks) and the Group Financial & Credit Risk Committee (credit/market/financial risks including climate and environmental). Specialized functions (Group Strategy & ESG, Group Stakeholder Engagement, Group ESG, Group Risk Management with Climate Risk & Risk Governance and Climate & Environmental Credit Analysis) embed climate and ESG into strategy, risk frameworks, origination, and credit review. ESG Advisory within Group Client Solutions supports client transition strategies and ESG communications; ESG expertise is distributed across functions and geographies.

- Business conduct: The Board approves the Group Code of Conduct anchored in UniCredit values (integrity, ownership, caring). A yearly “Tone from the Top” program promotes compliance and risk awareness; 2024 topics included unfair commercial practices, financial sanctions, ESG-sensitive sectors, AML/confidential & inside information, data protection, and digital risk.

- Governance of material IROs (GOV-2): 2024 marked the first CSRD-aligned double materiality assessment. The Board reviewed outcomes in November 2024. Processes to formalize frequency and methodology of oversight are being developed, with plans to institutionalize regular reviews. Climate risk (E1) and cybersecurity risk (S4) were confirmed material following expert review.

- Incentives linking pay and sustainability (GOV-3): The 2025 Group Incentive System is a Sustainable Performance Plan with short- and long-term conditions, a bonus-pool approach, strong pay-for-performance links, and shareholder alignment (share-based, deferrals). CEO’s 2025 scorecard: 80% financial, 20% non-financial; for CEO and selected leaders, 60% of bonus is deferred with long-term conditions (2026–2028), where Sustainability (incl. climate/Net Zero) has 20% weight. Goals include ESG business penetration, DE&I progress, and Net Zero 2030 targets embedded in RAF. Objectives cascade to Group Material Risk Takers; all GMRT short-term scorecards include at least one ESG KPI from a standardized “KPI Bluebook.” Non-executive directors receive only fixed remuneration.

- Due diligence statement (GOV-4): Due diligence is embedded in strategy and operations, not a standalone process. The double materiality assessment identified material negative impacts in climate change (GHG emissions), circular economy (resource use/waste), and consumers/end-users (data breaches). Management is addressed through policies, actions, targets, and metrics.

- Internal controls over sustainability reporting (GOV-5): A COSO-aligned internal control system (updated for “Internal Control over Sustainability Reporting,” March 2023) ensures integrity, completeness, and reliability of sustainability disclosures. A Sustainability Reporting Manager was appointed for 2024. Controls include entity-level governance and process-level controls (materiality, data collection, reconciliation). Risk/control assessments, testing, documentation, and remediation are performed, with reporting to the Board and Audit Committee. Subsidiaries provide internal certifications to the Parent.

- Strategy and value proposition (SBM-1): UniCredit is a pan-European commercial bank serving ~15 million clients via 13 banks across Italy, Germany, and Central & Eastern Europe, offering tailored advisory, financing, risk management, payments, investments, and insurance. Headcount is ~75,265 across regions. The Group has no revenues from ESRS-flagged sectors (fossil fuels, chemical production, controversial weapons, tobacco). ESG goals are embedded in client, people, and shareholder strategies, with a corporate ESG offer spanning green/social financing, sustainability-linked instruments, ESG advisory, strategic partnerships (e.g., Open-es), and risk management solutions to support client transition.

nodes.title: Strategy
nodes.heading: 2.1.3 Strategy
nodes.start_phrase: UniCredit is a pan-European Commercial Bank .
nodes.summary:
- Governance and internal controls for sustainability reporting: integrated risk assessments; Sustainability Reporting Manager reports to the Board and Audit Committee; subsidiaries provide internal certifications; defined roles, periodic updates, and remediation tracking.
- Business overview and markets: pan-European commercial bank serving ~15 million clients across Italy, Germany, Central and Eastern Europe; headcount distribution provided; no operations in ESRS-designated controversial sectors.
- ESG product offering and targets: corporate green/social financing, sustainability-linked solutions, ESG advisory, strategic partnerships (e.g., Open-es), transition risk management tools; individual products for energy-efficient home renovation and inclusive finance plus an ESG AUM catalogue; penetration targets for 2025–2027 of 15% ESG lending, 15% sustainable bonds, 50% ESG investment products.
- ESG strategy and enablers: principles-based approach aligned to Group values; goals aligned to net-zero; strategic levers (Championing Social, Enhanced Client Support via Net Zero plan, Beyond Climate, Evidencing Accountability); enablers (expanded ESG offering, lean governance, robust risk framework, empowered culture).
- Business model and value creation: client-centric model across four regions with three product factories (Corporate, Individual, Payment Solutions); payments ambition reinforced by a Mastercard partnership and expanded digital portal; value creation leveraging five capitals.
- Value chain mapping: upstream (capital providers, technology/data suppliers, regulators); downstream (retail, corporate, wealth clients; fintech/payment partners, asset managers and insurers); UniCredit’s intermediary role enabling capital flow, risk management, and economic activity.
- Stakeholder engagement and materiality: structured engagement with clients, employees, investors/shareholders, regulators, communities using NPS and multiple feedback tools; proactive policy engagement on sustainable finance; enhanced dialogue with NGOs (e.g., ESG Day); double materiality assessment informing strategy with Board oversight; strong human rights commitment.
- Climate and environmental management: double materiality inside-out/outside-in lens; integration of climate risk into models, provisioning (ECL), scenario analysis and ICAAP with resilience across time horizons; net-zero commitments (own emissions by 2030, financed emissions by 2050); sector policies restricting financing of thermal coal and high-impact oil & gas; advisory to support client transition; operational targets on renewable electricity, energy/water efficiency, circularity, mobility, and responsible sourcing.
- Nature-related and circular economy initiatives: portfolio-level impact and dependency assessments on biodiversity, pollution, water, and waste using recognized tools (e.g., ENCORE, TNFD) and heatmaps; participation in Finance for Biodiversity Pledge and UNEP FI Nature Guidance; membership in Ellen MacArthur Foundation; monitoring Water Usage Effectiveness in data centers; furniture reuse; client awareness on water and waste.
- Social topics: people strategy focused on wellbeing, DE&I, skills and development, fair employment, social dialogue, and industrial relations (including EWC); only positive material impacts/opportunities identified for own workforce; value-chain worker protections (human rights focus, UK Modern Slavery Act compliance).
- Communities and customers: commitments to financial inclusion and health (UNEP FI PRB), 2025 youth targets; tailored solutions for vulnerable groups; broad financial education initiatives; strengthened data privacy and cybersecurity; responsible marketing aligned with IAP/UPA and regulatory reviews (e.g., CONSOB).
- Business conduct and integrity: cultural transformation anchored in values; whistleblowing policy with protections; supplier standards (ILO and environmental policy); anti-bribery and corruption framework (Global Rules, Italian L.D. 231/01, Code of Conduct).
- Material IROs: detailed tables of impacts, risks, and opportunities across ESRS topics (E1–E5, S1–S4, G1), covering emissions (Scopes 1–3), green finance opportunities, physical climate credit risk, water and biodiversity, resource use and waste, workforce wellbeing/DE&I/training, human rights in the value chain, financial inclusion, privacy/cyber risks and reputational/operational risks, supplier practices, and anti-corruption; each with value-chain location and time horizons.
- IRO identification process: top-down ESRS-based double materiality at Group level, contextual analysis, extensive stakeholder engagement, gross impact assessment prior to mitigation, alignment with due diligence; no entity-specific IROs identified for the period.

nodes.title: Impact, risk and opportunity management
nodes.heading: 2.1.4 Impact, risk and opportunity management
nodes.start_phrase: The process to identify impacts, risks and opportunities was based on a top -down approach: UniCredit Holding identified a list of material IROs which has been shared with Legal Entities, and compared to their list, in order to guarantee coherence along the entire Group.
nodes.summary:
- Context: Excerpt from UniCredit’s 2024 Annual Reports and Accounts (Sustainability Statements), presenting the continued “List of Material Impacts, Risks and Opportunities (IROs)” aligned to ESRS topics, and the IRO-1 methodology for identifying and assessing them.

- ESRS S4 – Consumers and end-users:
  - Privacy:
    - Opportunity: Build long-term customer relationships via strong, safe ICT systems (downstream, medium-term).
    - Negative impact (potential): Customer data breaches and poor cybersecurity (downstream, medium-term).
    - Risks: Operational losses from unauthorized data access/cyberattacks; reputational risk from failing to protect data and meet user needs (own operations).
  - Privacy, Freedom of expression, Access to quality information:
    - Positive impact (potential): Business model transformation through digitalization, new tech, cloud, and AI (downstream, medium-term).
    - Opportunity: Market share expansion and retention via digital/innovative solutions (downstream, medium-term).
    - Opportunity: Stronger loyalty through optimized privacy, data security, and quality information (downstream, short-term).
    - Positive impact (actual): More informed customer decisions via transparent, neutral, fair advice and feedback mechanisms (downstream, medium-term).
  - Social inclusion/responsible marketing:
    - Opportunity (actual): Better client and shareholder relationships through clear, transparent communication (downstream, short-term).
  - Non-discrimination/access to products and services:
    - Positive impact (actual): Improved satisfaction and user experience by meeting expectations (downstream, medium-term).

- ESRS G1 – Business conduct:
  - Corporate culture:
    - Positive impacts (actual): Promote fair competition and reduce aggressive tax practices/evasion (upstream, medium-term); maximize value creation and distribution to stakeholders (across, medium-term).
  - Protection of whistle-blowers:
    - Positive impact (actual): Strengthen ethical culture across management, employees, partners (own operations, medium-term).
  - Supplier relationships and payment practices:
    - Positive impact (actual): Solid supplier relations and adherence to terms (upstream, medium-term).
    - Opportunity (actual): Higher quality purchases via a more sustainable, certified supply chain (upstream, medium-term).
  - Corruption and bribery:
    - Positive impact (actual): Prevention/detection through training for employees, top management, and stakeholders (upstream).
    - Risk: Money laundering, sanctions violations, bribery/corruption, KYC failures (across, medium-term).
    - Opportunity: Reputation enhancement by investing in innovative anti-corruption tools (both operations and value chain, medium-term).

- IRO-1 – Process to identify and assess material IROs:
  - Approach: Top-down, Group-led list shared with legal entities for coherence; focus on core banking activity while covering all entities in the Sustainability Statement perimeter.
  - Double materiality: Internal/external context analysis, mapping dependencies/resources/geographies, stakeholder mapping.
  - Stakeholder engagement: Questionnaires, workshops, forums, interviews, surveys; external perspectives integrated.
  - ESRS alignment: Screened ESRS 1-AR 16 matters; reconciled topics/sub-topics; tagged each impact by location (own ops/value chain), time horizon (short/medium/long), and strategic actors (e.g., employees, customers, shareholders).
  - Assessment principles: Considered gross impacts before mitigation; did not net positive against negative impacts; integrated due diligence outcomes for negative impacts (referenced GOV-4).

nodes.title: Description of the processes to identify and assess material impacts, risks and opportunities
nodes.heading: IRO-1 - Description of the processes to identify and assess material impacts, risks and opportunities
nodes.start_phrase: The process to identify impacts, risks and opportunities was based on a top -down approach: UniCredit Holding identified a list of material IROs which has been shared with Legal Entities, and compared to their list, in order to guarantee coherence along the entire Group.
nodes.summary:
- Scope and context: Extract from UniCredit’s 2024 Sustainability Statement outlining material Impacts, Risks and Opportunities (IROs) under ESRS, with a focus on consumers/end-users (S4), business conduct (G1), and the Group’s CSRD‑aligned double materiality process.

- Material IROs – S4 Consumers and end-users:
  - Privacy and cybersecurity: opportunities from strong ICT, data security and client loyalty; risks of data breaches, cyber attacks, operational and reputational impacts.
  - Freedom of expression and access to quality information: positive impacts from digitalisation, cloud and AI; opportunities to expand market share and retention through innovative digital services; improved client loyalty via privacy/data security and transparent, fair advice enabling customer feedback.
  - Social inclusion/responsible marketing: opportunities from clear, transparent communication; positive impacts on customer satisfaction and experience; better access to products and services.

- Material IROs – G1 Business conduct:
  - Corporate culture and fair competition: positive impacts from responsible tax practices; value creation and distribution to stakeholders.
  - Whistle-blower protection: positive cultural impacts across own operations.
  - Supplier relationships/payment practices: positive impacts from solid relationships and on-time payments; opportunity to improve purchased product/service quality via sustainable, certified supply chains.
  - Anti-corruption and bribery: positive impacts from prevention/detection and training; risks across AML/sanctions/bribery/KYC; opportunity to enhance reputation through innovative monitoring/prevention tools.

- IRO identification and assessment process (IRO‑1):
  - Top‑down, Group‑led list aligned to core banking activities; applied across all entities.
  - Context analysis and stakeholder mapping; reconciliation with ESRS topics and assignment of location (own operations/upstream/downstream), time horizon, and stakeholders.
  - Stakeholder engagement: internal (ESG, Reporting, Risk, Compliance, Top Management, Board) and external (employees, clients, investors, NGOs, academics, regulators, ESG raters) via interviews, surveys, workshops and desktop analysis.
  - Impact scoring: severity (scale, scope, irremediability for negatives) and likelihood; numerical 1–4 scoring; human rights negatives weighted for severity; materiality threshold set to focus on most relevant impacts; aggregation to sustainability matters by maximum score.
  - Risk/opportunity financial materiality: magnitude and likelihood (1–4); risks assessed by Group Risk Management (quantitative for climate; qualitative with data inputs for other E/S/G); opportunities assessed by Top Management (qualitative brand/competitiveness plus quantitative net profit potential); thresholds capture low‑probability/high‑impact and already‑present risks.
  - Integration: sustainability risks embedded in overall risk management (Risk Appetite, ICAAP, credit/market strategies, liquidity, models, provisioning, controversial sector policies, business continuity, reputational and litigation); opportunities integrated into product/financing innovation and strategic offerings in ESG.
  - Governance and controls: consistency/completeness checks, ESRS 2 compliance, legal entity feedback, Top Management confirmation, Board approval.

- Inputs and tools:
  - Internal: strategy, risk inventory, policies, Annual/Statutory/Integrated Reports, budget and planning frameworks.
  - External: ESG ratings/indices, EU regulations, media; Datamaran analytics; peer benchmarking; PRB, WEF Global Risks Report 2024, S&P Yearbook 2023, UNEP FI Impact Radar, OECD Guidelines.
  - Note: 2024 is first CSRD‑aligned double materiality cycle; not comparable to prior year.

- Environmental topics overview:
  - Climate change: recognition of Scope 1, 2, 3 emissions; support for green transition via financing energy efficiency, renewables, decarbonisation products/services, green tech start‑ups, and potential carbon trading; links to Notes on climate/environmental risks and scenarios.
  - Pollution, water, biodiversity, circular economy: screening shows low significance from own operations; limited exposure in construction/agriculture; no sites in/near biodiversity‑sensitive areas; opportunities for efficiency, recycling/reuse, dematerialisation and water monitoring/compliance.
  - Value chain assessment: sector heatmap of loan portfolio for nature‑related impacts/dependencies; negative impacts from financing high‑impact sectors largely non‑material except E5 (circular economy); environmental compliance/creditworthiness risks deemed non‑material; opportunities to scale green/sustainable financing.
  - Stakeholder engagement: ESG Day and external reviews (NGOs, academics, investors, clients) to validate environmental IROs.

nodes.title: Climate Change:
nodes.heading: Climate Change :
nodes.start_phrase: UniCredit acknowledges that its activities and business generate greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions, both directly through its ow n energy consumption (Scope 1 and 2) and indirectly across its upstream and downstream activities (Scope 3).
nodes.summary:
- Focus: UniCredit’s 2024 Sustainability Statement within the Consolidated Report describes how sustainability-related impacts, risks and opportunities (IROs) are identified, assessed, managed, and embedded across the Group’s risk and strategy frameworks, aligned with ESRS and CSRD requirements.

- Embedding sustainability in risk management:
  - Sustainability-related risks prioritized via financial materiality and stakeholder input.
  - Full integration into Risk Appetite, ICAAP, credit and market risk strategies, liquidity, credit models and provisioning, and non-financial risk controls (controversial sectors, business continuity, reputational risk, litigation).

- ESG opportunities and strategic integration:
  - Material opportunities centered on ESG-driven product and service innovation, particularly financing solutions.
  - Positioning ESG offerings to meet market demand and support environmental and social objectives, targeting long-term value creation.

- Governance and assurance of the process:
  - Top Management applied a structured, control-focused approach to ensure consistency with Standards.
  - Verification of topic completeness, stakeholder coverage across the value chain, and cross-checks with prior years.
  - Compliance review with ESRS 2 and topical standards; feedback from all Legal Entities considered.
  - Final list of material IROs presented to the Board of Directors.

- IROs identification inputs:
  - Internal: business strategy, activities, client solutions, Annual/Statutory/Integrated Reports, ESG policies, Group Inventory Risk, ESG ratings/indices, regulations, media.
  - External: Datamaran scan of 100+ ESG topics, peer benchmarking, PRB, WEF Global Risks Report 2024, S&P Yearbook 2023, UNEP FI Impact Radar, OECD Guidelines.
  - Ongoing stakeholder engagement through multiple channels.

- IROs assessment approach:
  - Use of ICAAP, management control, strategic planning, business model considerations, and budgeting.
  - 2024 marks first CSRD-aligned double materiality process with deeper financial materiality; results not comparable to prior year.

- Climate change:
  - Recognition of direct (Scope 1–2) and indirect (Scope 3) emissions.
  - Actions: financing energy efficiency and renewables; enhancing awareness and commitments.
  - Opportunities: green project financing, decarbonization products/services for clients, support for green tech start-ups, potential entry into carbon trading.
  - Cross-references to consolidated accounts for climate/environmental risk and scenario compatibility disclosures.

- Other environmental topics (pollution; water and marine resources; biodiversity and ecosystems; resource use and circular economy):
  - Operational screening indicates the Bank’s own activities are not highly impactful; no sites near biodiversity-sensitive areas.
  - Factors assessed: travel-related pollution, water management, resource/raw material use, waste, ecosystem contamination/biodiversity loss (limited relevance from small exposure to construction/agriculture).
  - Opportunities: cost savings via efficiency, recycling/reuse, dematerialization, and water monitoring/compliance.
  - Conclusion: environmental impacts and related risks from own operations are not significant; no significant biodiversity transition/physical/systemic risks identified.

- Client and portfolio perspective:
  - Sector-level heatmap of the loan portfolio to gauge nature-related risks via impacts and dependencies.
  - Negative impacts from financing polluting, water-intensive, resource-heavy, waste-generating, and biodiversity-affecting sectors—assessed as non-material except for E5 (circular economy), which is material.
  - Positive influence through client engagement and awareness-raising.
  - Opportunities to expand green/sustainable financial products and services supporting natural capital.
  - Risks from counterparty non-compliance with environmental laws and potential credit deterioration in sensitive sectors—assessed as non-material.

- Stakeholder engagement:
  - ESG Day held to gather stakeholder perspectives on environmental IROs.
  - External stakeholders (NGOs, academics, investors, clients) reviewed identified IROs to ensure a comprehensive assessment.

nodes.title: Anti-fraud policy:
nodes.heading: Anti-fraud policy :

- Procurement scope: Supplier qualification applies when Group Procurement centrally manages negotiations/purchases; acknowledges some categories/thresholds are handled outside Procurement.
- Expenditure regulation: Defines principles and minimum requirements for end-to-end management of expenditures and investments (demand-to-pay); classifies expenditures (P&L impact) vs. investments (long-term, multi-year utility).

nodes.title: Supplier qualification process:

Objectives include selecting compliant, sustainable and financially sound suppliers; managing third-party risks (e.g., corruption, reputational, economic); promoting ethical and sustainability principles; and maintaining a list of qualified suppliers for Procurement-led sourcing. Screening uses external risk scores plus Procurement/Compliance checks (anti-corruption, negative news); when scores are unavailable, uses questionnaires including environmental and social aspects; includes periodic reviews and continuous risk monitoring.

Clarifies classifications (expenditures affecting P&L vs multi-year investments). Roles: Group Cost Management (steers approval process, monitors Group and UniCredit S.p.A. NHR costs, manages ICT demand and Projects & Expenses Committee activities) and Group Procurement (centralized purchasing for cost optimization).

nodes.title: Expenditure regulation:
nodes.heading: Expenditure regulation :
nodes.start_phrase: This global policy has the purpose to define principles and minimum requirements necessary to manage expenditures and investm ents, from demand to pay.
nodes.summary:
- Scope and governance: A Group-wide policy, approved by the CEO, applies to all UniCredit legal entities, governing bodies, employees, tied agents, and temporary staff, to be implemented in line with local laws, adopting the stricter local requirements where applicable.
- Anti-fraud policy: Establishes a fraud management system for all Group entities to identify, assess, and proactively mitigate internal and external fraud risks; defines roles and responsibilities; aligns with EU Directive 2015/2366; Group Security oversees implementation.
- Supplier qualification: Aligned with ILO Core Conventions and UN Global Compact principles; sets third‑party screening criteria before sourcing; aims to select compliant, sustainable, and financially sound suppliers, manage third‑party risks (e.g., corruption, reputational, economic), promote ethical and sustainability standards, and maintain a qualified supplier list for Procurement-led sourcing.
- Supplier screening mechanics: Centralized by Group Procurement for centrally managed purchases; uses external risk provider scores, anti‑corruption and adverse news checks by Procurement/Compliance; relies on questionnaires (including environmental/social aspects) when data are unavailable; includes periodic reviews and incident/risk score change monitoring.
- Expenditure regulation: Defines principles/minimum requirements for managing expenditures and investments from demand to payment; distinguishes P&L expenditures from multi‑year investments.
- Roles in spending: Group Cost Management steers Group-level approvals, monitors Group and UniCredit S.p.A. NHR costs, manages Group ICT demand, and PEC activities; Group Procurement centrally manages purchases to optimize costs.
- EU Taxonomy Article 8 disclosure: Presents methodology and KPIs for Taxonomy eligibility/alignment, enhancing transparency and supporting the transition to a low‑carbon economy; focuses on the Green Asset Ratio (GAR).
- GAR results: 2024 Turnover-based GAR is 1.36% on €547bn total GAR assets (vs. 1.16% on €551bn in 2023), mainly driven by climate change mitigation exposures; acknowledges data gaps due to reliance on counterparties subject to NFRD.
- Calculation perimeter and exclusions: Includes only undertakings with mandatory NFRD disclosures; excludes exposures to central governments, central banks, and supranational issuers; uses only counterparty KPIs (no use‑of‑proceeds within Article 8 templates); T‑1 templates published but not fully comparable due to perimeter changes.
- Methodology for corporates and guarantees: Uses weighted averages of financing activities and counterparties’ Taxonomy-aligned activity shares; sources NFRD reports via an external provider; applies parent company KPIs where relevant; if CCM/CCA breakdown is missing, values are included in total columns, which may exceed component sums.
- Mortgages to households: For collateralized loans, assesses “Acquisition” perimeter under Delegated Regulation 2021/2139; excludes “Renovation” and motor vehicles due to data limitations; identifies “green loans” using Energy Performance Certificate and Primary Energy Demand data for eligibility KPIs.

nodes.start_phrase: The following tables display the disclosure obligations under Article 8 of the Disclosures Delegated Act supplementing the EU Taxonomy Regulation (2020/852), which requires financial companies to report Taxonomy eligibility and alignment’s key performance indicators (KPIs), starting for calendar year 2023.
nodes.summary:
- Group-wide policy governance: A CEO-approved policy applies across all UniCredit legal entities, covering governing bodies, employees, tied agents, and temporary staff. It must comply with local laws, with more restrictive local requirements taking precedence.
- Anti-fraud policy: Establishes a fraud management system to identify, assess, and proactively address internal and external fraud risks, clarifying roles and responsibilities. It incorporates requirements from EU Directive 2015/2366, applies to UniCredit S.p.A. and all Group entities, and is implemented by Group Security.
- Supplier qualification: Aligned with ILO Fundamental Conventions and UN Global Compact principles, the process screens third parties before sourcing. Objectives include selecting suppliers on compliance, sustainability, and financial criteria; managing third-party risks (e.g., corruption, reputational, economic); promoting ethical and sustainability principles; and maintaining a qualified supplier list. Group Procurement leads when purchases are centralized; some categories/thresholds sit outside Procurement.
- Supplier screening methods: Uses external risk scores plus Procurement/Compliance checks (anti-corruption, adverse news). If external scores are unavailable, uses supplier questionnaires covering environmental and social aspects. Qualifications are periodically reviewed, with ongoing monitoring for incidents or risk score changes.
- Expenditure regulation: A global policy governs expenditures and investments from demand to pay. Expenditures affect P&L; investments are long-term with multi-year utility. Key roles: Group Cost Management (approval steering, cost monitoring, ICT demand, Projects & Expenses Committee) and Group Procurement (central purchasing and cost optimization).
- EU Taxonomy Article 8 disclosure: Presents eligibility/alignment KPIs and the Green Asset Ratio (GAR) to enhance sustainability transparency and support transition to a low-carbon economy. Only undertakings subject to NFRD are included; exposures to central governments, central banks, and supranationals are excluded. Use-of-proceeds information is not included in Article 8 templates.
- GAR results: Turnover-based GAR is 1.36% on total GAR assets of €547bn, up from 1.16% on €551bn at year-end 2023, driven mainly by climate change mitigation exposures.
- Calculation approach: Portfolio segmented by asset class with differing methods as required. T-1 templates are published, but comparisons are not meaningful due to a changed 2024 perimeter.
- Methodology for corporates and guarantees: KPIs are a weighted average of financing activities and counterparties’ Taxonomy-aligned activity shares. NFRD entities include those meeting criteria directly or indirectly; where a counterparty contributes to a parent’s KPIs, the parent’s KPIs are used. If counterparties do not split KPIs by objective (e.g., CCM vs CCA), values are recorded in TOTAL columns, which may exceed the sum of components.
- Household collateralized loans: Focuses on the “Acquisition” perimeter (excludes “Renovation” and motor vehicles due to data gaps). “Green loans” are identified using EPC and PED data per Delegated Regulation 2021/2139 for eligibility.

nodes.start_phrase: The following tables display the disclosure obligations under Article 8 of the Disclosures Delegated Act supplementing the EU Taxonomy Regulation (2020/852), which requires financial companies to report Taxonomy eligibility and alignment’s key performance indicators (KPIs), starting for calendar year 2023.
nodes.summary:
- Scope and governance of Group policies: A CEO-approved Group-wide policy applies to all UniCredit legal entities, governing bodies, employees, and tied/temporary staff, with local laws prevailing where more restrictive.
- Anti-fraud policy: Establishes a Group fraud management system for identifying, assessing, and managing internal and external fraud risks; defines roles and responsibilities; incorporates EU Directive 2015/2366 requirements; Group Security oversees implementation.
- Supplier qualification process: Aligned with ILO Fundamental Conventions and UN Global Compact; sets third-party screening criteria to select suppliers based on compliance, sustainability, and financial soundness; manages third-party risks (e.g., corruption, reputational); promotes ethical and sustainability principles; maintains qualified supplier lists. Screening uses external risk scores, Procurement/Compliance checks (anti-corruption, adverse news), or supplier questionnaires (including environmental and social aspects) when scores are unavailable; periodic reviews and ongoing risk monitoring are required. Not all purchases are centrally managed by Procurement.
- Expenditure regulation: Defines principles and minimum requirements to manage expenditures and investments from demand to pay across all Group entities. Distinguishes P&L-impacting expenditures from multi-year investments. Roles: Group Cost Management (approval process steering, monitoring Group and UniCredit S.p.A. NHR costs, ICT demand, Projects & Expenses Committee) and Group Procurement (centralized purchasing for cost optimization).
- EU Taxonomy Article 8 disclosures: Presents methodology and KPIs for Taxonomy eligibility/alignment, including the Green Asset Ratio (GAR). For 2024, GAR Turnover-based is 1.36% on €547bn GAR assets (vs. 1.16% on €551bn in 2023), mainly driven by climate change mitigation exposures. Only NFRD-reporting undertakings are included; exposures to central governments, central banks, and supranationals are excluded; data gaps arise where counterparties lack mandatory non-financial disclosure.
- Calculation approach: 
  - For financial/non-financial corporations and financial guarantees, KPIs use a weighted average of financing activities and counterparties’ Taxonomy-aligned activity shares, leveraging NFRD reports collected via an external provider. Subsidiaries may inherit parent KPIs; where no objective breakdown is provided, totals are captured under the overall “TOTAL” column, which may exceed the sum of components.
  - For household collateralized loans, the focus is on the “Acquisition” perimeter under Delegated Regulation 2021/2139; “Renovation” and “Motor vehicles” are excluded due to data limitations. “Green loans” are identified using EPC and PED criteria for eligibility. 
  - T-1 templates are published but not comparable year-over-year due to changes in the 2024 disclosure perimeter.

nodes.title: Our calculation approach
nodes.heading: Our calculation approach
nodes.start_phrase: In accordance with the templates provided by Regulation, for the calculation of the GAR KPIs, we have differentiated the portf olio by assets and applied different calculation approaches, where required.
nodes.summary:
- Group-wide policy governance: A CEO-approved policy applies to all UniCredit Group legal entities, governing bodies, employees, tied agents, and temporary staff, with stricter local laws prevailing over group principles.
- Anti-fraud policy: Establishes a fraud management system for all entities to identify, assess, and manage internal/external fraud risks, protect assets, and define roles and responsibilities; incorporates EU Directive 2015/2366 requirements; Group Security oversees implementation.
- Supplier qualification process: Aligned with ILO Fundamental Conventions and UN Global Compact; sets pre-sourcing screening criteria to select suppliers on compliance, sustainability, and financial soundness; manages third-party risks (e.g., corruption, reputational, economic) by excluding unqualified suppliers; promotes ethical and sustainability principles; maintains a list of qualified suppliers. Screening leverages external risk scores, Procurement/Compliance checks (anti-corruption, adverse news), and fallback questionnaires (including environmental and social aspects); includes periodic reviews and incident monitoring. Purchases are centrally managed by Group Procurement where applicable, with some categories/thresholds handled outside Procurement.
- Expenditure regulation: Defines principles and minimum requirements to manage expenditures and investments from demand to pay across all legal entities. Classifies disbursements into expenditures (P&L impact) and investments (long-term, multi-year utility). Key roles: Group Cost Management (steers approvals, monitors Group and UniCredit S.p.A. costs, manages ICT demand, supports the Projects & Expenses Committee) and Group Procurement (central purchasing for cost optimization).
- EU Taxonomy Article 8 disclosure: Presents eligibility and alignment KPIs to enhance sustainability transparency, chiefly via the Green Asset Ratio (GAR). Data depend on counterparties’ mandatory non-financial disclosures, with non-reporting entities excluded, creating data gaps.
- 2024 results: Turnover-based GAR is 1.36% on €547bn total GAR assets, up from 1.16% on €551bn at year-end 2023, driven mainly by climate change mitigation exposures.
- Methodology highlights: Portfolio segmented by asset type; only undertakings subject to NFRD included; exposures to central governments, central banks, and supranationals excluded; only counterparty KPIs used (no use-of-proceeds in Article 8 templates). T-1 templates are published but not comparable due to a changed perimeter. For financial and non-financial corporations and financial guarantees, KPIs reflect weighted averages of counterparties’ Taxonomy-aligned activities, using parent company KPIs where relevant; when no CCM/CCA split is reported, totals are used. For household-collateralized loans, only the “Acquisition” perimeter under Delegated Regulation 2021/2139 is considered; “Renovation” and “Motor vehicles” are excluded; green loan eligibility is based on EPC and Primary Energy Demand data for top-performing buildings.

nodes.title: Financial Corporations, Non-Financial Corporations, and Financial Guarantees
nodes.heading: • Financial Corporations, Non- Financial Corporations, and Financial Guarantees :
nodes.start_phrase: the Taxonomy KPIs consist of the weighted average of financing activities and the proportion of Taxonomy -aligned economic activities of the counterparty.
nodes.summary:
- Group-wide policy framework: Policies approved by the CEO apply to all UniCredit Group legal entities, governing bodies, employees, tied agents and temps, and across all business activities, with stricter local laws prevailing where applicable.

- Anti-fraud policy: Establishes a fraud management system for identifying, assessing and mitigating internal and external fraud risks; clarifies roles and responsibilities within fraud governance; aligns with EU Directive 2015/2366; Group Security oversees implementation.

- Supplier qualification process: Aligned with ILO Fundamental Conventions and UN Global Compact; sets third‑party screening criteria before sourcing. Objectives include selecting compliant, sustainable, and financially sound suppliers; managing third‑party risks (corruption, reputational, economic); promoting ethical and sustainability principles; and maintaining an approved supplier list. Screening leverages external risk scores plus Procurement/Compliance controls (anti‑corruption, adverse news). Where scores are unavailable, questionnaires (including environmental and social aspects) are used. Reviews are periodic with ongoing risk monitoring. Central purchasing is managed by Group Procurement, though some categories/thresholds are handled outside Procurement.

- Expenditure regulation: Defines principles and minimum requirements for end‑to‑end management of expenditures and investments. Distinguishes P&L expenditures from multi‑year investments. Key roles:
  - Group Cost Management: steers approval processes, monitors Group and UniCredit S.p.A. non‑HR costs, manages Group ICT demand, and supports the Projects & Expenses Committee (PEC).
  - Group Procurement: centralizes purchasing to optimize costs.

- Environmental information (EU Taxonomy Article 8 disclosure):
  - Purpose: Provide transparency on Taxonomy eligibility and alignment via key KPIs, chiefly the Green Asset Ratio (GAR).
  - GAR result: Turnover‑based GAR of 1.36% on €547bn total GAR assets (vs. 1.16% on €551bn in 2023), mainly driven by climate change mitigation exposures.
  - Scope and data approach: Includes only NFRD‑mandated undertakings; excludes central governments, central banks, supranationals. Uses counterparties’ disclosed KPIs; “use of proceeds” not included in Article 8 templates. T‑1 templates published but not comparable due to scope changes in 2024.
  - Methodology:
    - For financial and non‑financial corporates and financial guarantees: weighted average of financing activities and counterparties’ Taxonomy‑aligned shares; data collected with an external provider. Parent company KPIs used when subsidiaries contribute to parent disclosures. If counterparties don’t split KPIs by objective, values are placed in total columns, which may exceed the sum of components.
    - Loans collateralized to households: Focus on “Acquisition” perimeter under Delegated Regulation 2021/2139; excludes “Renovation” and “Motor vehicles” due to data limits. Green loans identified using EPC and Primary Energy Demand criteria for top‑performing buildings.
  - Data gaps: Non‑NFRD entities are excluded, which lowers coverage and impacts the ratio.

nodes.title: Additional disclosure on Nuclear and Gas related activities
nodes.heading: • Additional disclosure on Nuclear and Gas related activities :
nodes.start_phrase: we have disclosed the eligibility, non -eligibility, and alignment of nuclear energy and fossil gas related activities in accordance with Article 8(6), (7) and (8) of the amended Disclosures Delegated Act as of 1 January 2023.
nodes.summary:
- Purpose and scope: Extract from UniCredit’s 2024 Annual Reports and Accounts, Sustainability statements, providing EU Taxonomy Article 8 disclosures for credit institutions, including methodologies and detailed quantitative KPIs (GAR stock and flow, off-balance sheet KPIs), with Annex VI templates.

- Methodology highlights:
  - Real estate alignment: For assets built before Dec 31, 2020, only documented EPC=A counted; for Italy, Top-15% energy performance approach applied; for assets built after Dec 31, 2020, NZEB (Nearly Zero Energy Building) approach used. Regional NZEB and Top-15% data sourced from an external provider. Conservative stance (only adequate documentation considered).
  - DNSH assessment: Integrates analysis of physical climate risks aligned with thresholds and climate data used in Pillar 3 Template 5; excludes adaptation plans or other mitigating actions for conservatism.
  - Household vehicles: Eligible exposures are loans for motor vehicle purchases; aligned exposures limited to low-emission vehicles.
  - Assets under Management (AuM): Perimeter based on collective investment funds disclosed in Group external communications. Alignment calculated via weighted average of portfolio-level Taxonomy-aligned proportions using external provider data on underlying holdings’ KPIs. Total AuM includes all asset classes; “of which debt/equity” only includes those classes, so totals can exceed the sum of components.
  - New business (flow): Determined via transaction-level delta stock between Dec 31, 2024 and Dec 31, 2023 (new originations only).
  - Nuclear and gas: Eligibility, non-eligibility, and alignment disclosed per Article 8(6)-(8) of the amended Disclosures Delegated Act (effective Jan 1, 2023); KPIs calculated for NFRD-subject non-financial counterparties using most recent data.

- Summary KPIs (as presented):
  - Green Asset Ratio (GAR) stock: Total environmentally sustainable assets €7,432m; 1.36% turnover-based and 1.91% CapEx-based; coverage over total assets 68.99%; 56.10% of assets excluded from the numerator; 31.01% excluded from the denominator.
  - GAR flow: €2,208m; 2.19% turnover-based and 3.42% CapEx-based; coverage 26.94%.
  - Additional KPIs: Financial guarantees €291m (5.81% turnover-based; 10.73% CapEx-based). AuM €3,225m (9.22% turnover-based; 14.12% CapEx-based).

- Detailed GAR composition (turnover- and CapEx-based):
  - Comprehensive breakdowns by counterparty type (financial undertakings, non-financial undertakings, households, local governments), instrument (loans, debt securities including UoP, equity), and environmental objectives (CCM, CCA, WTR, CE, PPC, BIO), including use-of-proceeds, transitional, and enabling categories.
  - Households: Large eligible exposure primarily through residential mortgages; aligned portions include eligible building loans and low-emission vehicle loans.
  - Exclusions and coverage: Significant portions excluded from GAR numerator or denominator per Article 7 (e.g., SMEs and NFCs not subject to NFRD, non-EU non-NFRD counterparties). Assets not covered for GAR include central governments/supranationals, central bank exposures, and trading book items.

- Comparative view 2024 vs 2023:
  - Increase in Taxonomy-aligned amounts and ratios year over year (e.g., total aligned under turnover approach rising from €6,396m in 2023 to €7,432m in 2024; higher CapEx-based alignment).
  - Expanded off-balance sheet disclosures with higher eligible/aligned figures for financial guarantees and AuM.

- Data sourcing and conservatism: Reliance on external providers for building performance benchmarks and AuM portfolio KPIs; strict documentation requirements and exclusion of mitigation/adaptation plans emphasize conservative alignment measurement.

nodes.title: GAR sector information - Turnover based
nodes.heading: 2 GAR sector information - Turnover based
nodes.start_phrase: (€ million)
nodes.summary:
- Focus: EU Taxonomy Green Asset Ratio (GAR) disclosures within UniCredit’s Sustainability Statement of the 2024 Annual Reports and Accounts, as at 31.12.2024.
- Content type: Detailed, turnover-based sector breakdown (in € million) and related KPI percentages for assets in scope of GAR, following EU Taxonomy/NFRD/EBA templates.

What the tables cover
- GAR sector information – Turnover based:
  - Granular breakdown by NACE Rev. 2 four‑digit sectors for non‑financial corporates subject to NFRD.
  - For each sector: gross carrying amount and “of which environmentally sustainable” amounts mapped to the six EU Taxonomy environmental objectives:
    - Climate Change Mitigation (CCM)
    - Climate Change Adaptation (CCA)
    - Sustainable use and protection of Water and Marine Resources (WTR)
    - Transition to a Circular Economy (CE)
    - Pollution prevention and control (PPC)
    - Protection and restoration of Biodiversity and Ecosystems (BIO)
  - A total column consolidates environmentally sustainable amounts across all objectives.
  - Coverage spans manufacturing (chemicals, cement, metals, electronics, machinery, vehicles), utilities (electricity production/transmission/distribution, gas, steam), water and waste (water supply, waste collection/treatment, recovery), construction and civil engineering (buildings, roads, rail, utilities, water projects), transport (rail, road services, water), telecommunications and IT, real estate (buy/sell, rental and operating, management), professional and research services, leasing, and selected social care activities.
  - Illustrative sectors with notable environmentally sustainable amounts include:
    - Electricity: production, transmission and distribution (D35.x), showing significant CCM alignment and some contributions to other objectives.
    - Water and waste: water collection/treatment/supply (E36.00) spanning CCM, CCA, WTR; waste collection and treatment (E38.11/E38.21) with strong Circular Economy components.
    - Transport and infrastructure: rail construction and services (F42.12; H49.10/H49.20) and utility projects for electricity/telecom (F42.22) showing CCM alignment.
    - Manufacturing: basic iron and steel (C24.10), cement (C23.51), selected electrical/electronic equipment (C26–C27), machinery for paper production (C28.95), and motor vehicles (C29.10) with CCM and some CCA entries.
    - Real estate: rental/operating of own or leased real estate (L68.20) with material CCM/CCA totals.
    - Leasing of cars and light vehicles (N77.11) contributing to CCM.

- GAR KPI (stock) – Turnover based – Percentages:
  - Presents the proportion of total covered assets funding Taxonomy‑relevant (eligible) and Taxonomy‑aligned activities for CCM, CCA and WTR, including “of which” categories (use of proceeds, transitional, enabling, as applicable).
  - Breakdown by counterparty segments:
    - Financial undertakings (credit institutions, other financials, management companies, insurance undertakings)
    - Non‑financial undertakings
    - Households (including loans collateralised by residential property, building renovation loans, motor vehicle loans)
    - Local governments (housing and other)
    - Collateral obtained (residential and commercial real estate)
  - Headline indications:
    - Total GAR assets represent about 20.2% of total covered assets, with c.1.32% Taxonomy‑aligned for CCM, including identified use‑of‑proceeds, transitional and enabling portions.
    - Small but positive shares are reported for CCA and WTR eligibility/alignment.
    - Households show a sizable eligible share driven by mortgage exposure, with a measurable aligned component via use‑of‑proceeds.
    - Non‑financial corporates contribute to both eligible and aligned CCM shares; financial undertakings add smaller aligned portions mainly via securities and equity holdings.

Purpose and use
- Demonstrates UniCredit’s exposure to Taxonomy‑eligible and aligned activities at detailed sector level, quantifying environmentally sustainable financing by objective and aggregating to KPI percentages, in line with EU GAR disclosure requirements.

nodes.title: GAR KPI (stock) - Turnover based - % (compared to total covered assets in the denominator)
nodes.heading: 3 GAR KPI (stock) - Turnover based - % (compared to total covered assets in the denominator)
nodes.summary:
- The extract presents UniCredit’s EU Taxonomy Green Asset Ratio (GAR) stock disclosures within the Sustainability Statement of the 2024 Annual Reports and Accounts, detailing the share of total covered assets that fund taxonomy-relevant sectors, split between taxonomy-eligible and taxonomy-aligned activities.
- It provides turnover-based GAR KPIs as of 31.12.2024 and 31.12.2023 across the six environmental objectives (climate change mitigation, climate change adaptation, water and marine resources, circular economy, pollution prevention and control, biodiversity and ecosystems), with breakdowns by:
  - Counterparty/segment: financial undertakings (credit institutions, other financial corporations, management companies, insurance), non-financial undertakings, households, and local governments.
  - Asset class: loans and advances, debt securities (including use-of-proceeds instruments), equity instruments, and collateralized immovable properties.
  - Instrument type flags: of which use of proceeds, transitional, and enabling activities.
- 2024 turnover-based results highlight:
  - Total taxonomy-eligible assets: 20.46% of total covered assets; taxonomy-aligned: 1.36%.

nodes.title: Strategy
nodes.heading: 2.2.2.1 Strategy
nodes.start_phrase:
In line with the effort sustained in the previous year s, in 2024 UniCredit Group adopted a Transition Plan to support the achievement of our Net Zero
targets for f inanced and own emissions , and to convert our commitments into actions.
nodes.summary:
- EU Taxonomy non-eligible activities: Most turnover and capex in the KPI denominators are classified as “other taxonomy non-eligible” (≈79.5% of turnover; ≈79.0% of capex), with immaterial amounts in rows tied to specific Delegated Regulation sections.
- Climate strategy and transition plan (E1-1): UniCredit adopted a Group-wide Transition Plan in 2024 aligned with NZBA, GFANZ and CSRD E1, targeting Net Zero by 2050 and 2030 interim targets across six high-emitting sectors. Scope 1–2 (market-based) Net Zero by 2030; financed emissions (Scope 3, Cat. 15) aligned to Paris Agreement. Bank is not excluded from EU Paris-aligned benchmarks.
- Decarbonisation levers:
  - Own emissions: renewable electricity sourcing, space optimization, energy efficiency, and heating system transformation.
  - Financed emissions: sector-specific engagement, portfolio rebalancing, and support for transition technologies and projects.
- Sector strategies and examples:
  - Oil & Gas: client engagement on transition plans; shift financing toward alternative fuels; reduce most carbon-intensive activities; support hydrogen, biofuels, CCUS; sponsorships (World Hydrogen Congress) and membership (European Clean Hydrogen Alliance); financing biofuels/biomethane via infrastructure funds.
  - Power Generation: finance shift from fossil to renewables (wind, PV) via project finance; industry participation (Solar Association in CZ/SK; Climate & Sustainable Leaders).
  - Automotive: support electrification and value-chain opportunities (EV batteries, infrastructure); financing EV-only plant expansion for Mercedes-Benz in Hungary; “In Motion” value-chain approach.
  - Steel: signatory to Sustainable Steel Principles; support hydrogen/electrification pathways; MLA and lender to SACE-covered green loan for Salzgitter’s SALCOS project (DRI + EAF with green power/H2; targeted 95% emissions cut by 2033).
  - Shipping: align with IMO 2023 GHG strategy; finance next-gen vessels and retrofits; ongoing client engagement pending clearer global rules and fuel availability.
  - Commercial Real Estate: prioritize energy-efficient assets and retrofits; collect EPCs; financed Coima P39 (Nearly Zero Energy Building) in Milan; launched “One4Planet Green Buildings” loan in Italy.
  - Residential Real Estate: emphasize need for government incentives; launched “Mutuo Sostenibilità Energetica” mortgage in Italy (incl. EPC simulation; €83.3m disbursed by Dec 2024); new partnerships.
- Resources and enablement:
  - Group Net Zero program since 2022; cross-functional (ESG, Finance, Risk, Business, Digital), ~150 staff.
  - ICT upgrades for data pipelines, client transition-plan assessment, dashboards, deal/portfolio impact simulations, and tagging of transition finance; non-material ICT spend.
  - Group-wide training (Net Zero basics, client plan assessment, credit implications, transition finance); local expert teams and certified programs (e.g., Germany’s Sustainable Finance Experts).
- Business integration and governance:
  - Embedding Net Zero into planning, risk, and business processes; targets set at Group level, broken down and cascaded by division.
  - Net Zero KPIs included in Risk Appetite Framework; remuneration of Top Management linked to Net Zero KPIs.
  - Sector policies tightened to cease financing of most controversial carbon-intensive activities and phase out legacy exposure; ongoing policy updates.
  - Transition Plan approved by CEO, reviewed by Board (Feb 2024); 2030 targets similarly approved before disclosure.
- Implementation progress (2024):
  - Target setting: initial 2030 targets for Oil & Gas, Power, Automotive; added Steel (Jan 2024), Shipping and Commercial Real Estate (Jul 2024); 2022 baseline for Residential.
  - Monitoring: new process delivering periodic Net Zero impact reports to business; coverage expanded from initial sectors to Steel in 2024, with Shipping and Real Estate to follow by early 2025.
  - Risk management: Net Zero embedded in policies, RAF KPIs, credit strategies, and credit process; client clustering (leaders/aligning/laggards) with tailored engagement; greater use of green/transition finance.
  - Client transition-plan assessment: cross-industry questionnaire aligned to GFANZ, CDP, CA100+; scoring 0–100 into developed/early-stage/absent plans; piloted in 2024; plan to use external experts.
  - Products/services: green and sustainability-linked financing; public-program partnerships (KfW, EIF); internal definition of transition finance (EU Commission recommendations) codified in ESG Product Guidelines; third-party certification of client transition plans required for transition finance; ESG advisory supports origination and structuring.
  - Tools and partnerships: embedded assessment and steering tools; joined Open-es (with Cerved ESG scoring) to support client decarbonisation.
- Stakeholder dialogue:
  - Active in NZBA working groups; policy engagement via IIF, AFME, EBF on transition finance and planning.
  - Local collaborations (e.g., WWF Austria) to enhance sustainable product integration.
  - ESG Day 2024 with 13,000+ participants; launched “Skills for Transition” training program across six countries to upskill workforces for the green transition.
- Policies (E1-2): Climate policies address double materiality—impacts (Scopes 1–3), risks (notably credit risk from physical and transition factors), and opportunities (green investments/products, new markets). Smart Office Workplace policy drives operational footprint reduction; sector policies (Civil Nuclear, Coal, Defense, Mining, Oil & Gas, Tobacco, Water infrastructure) manage financed emissions and risk; ESG Product Guidelines define classification/reporting and guard against greenwashing.
- Actions and resources (E1-3) for own operations:
  - 2024 GHG inventory: Scope 1 = 24,412 tCO2e; Scope 2 market-based = 16,702 tCO2e (location-based = 100,830 tCO2e); Scope 3 (excl. Cat. 15) = 285,848 tCO2e; perimeter change limits comparability.
  - Continuous focus on space optimization, renewable electricity sourcing, energy efficiency in premises/data centers, and heating decarbonisation.

  - Residential Real Estate: baseline disclosed for 2022; intensity 35.8 kgCO2e/m2 in 2023 (−1.4% vs 36.3). Continued client support; government incentives seen as critical enablers.

Levers: renewable sourcing, space optimization, energy efficiency, heating transformation. Internal working group and staff engagement established.

- S3-4 (Actions and effectiveness): Ongoing social strategy across social finance, community contributions, and people support; effectiveness tracked through feedback, surveys, interviews, satisfaction, workshops, and awareness campaigns across countries.

nodes.heading: 2.4.1.2 Metrics and targets
nodes.start_phrase: The UniCredit group has zero tolerance for acts of corruption and prohibits them in any form, whether direct or indirect.
nodes.summary:
- Section from UniCredit’s 2024 Annual Reports and Accounts (Sustainability Statement) detailing the Group’s anti-bribery and anti-corruption (ABC) program and payment practices.
- ABC framework:
  - Comprehensive internal regulations for risk areas (public officials, gifts and hospitality, third-party engagement, donations/sponsorships/memberships, HR, M&A).
  - Tools for documenting/approving gifts and hospitality above thresholds and for due diligence on third parties and beneficiaries; creation of an anti-corruption register of external suppliers; automated due diligence within a decentralized process.
  - Independent second-level controls by a dedicated compliance function; regular reporting of compliance risk assessments and internal audit reviews to internal control committees.
  - Governance and oversight: Group Anti-Corruption Officer and a specialized team within Compliance to advise, implement policies, review cases, and support investigations; annual compliance reporting to the Board and ad hoc reporting to top management; whistleblowing channels available.
  - Training: mandatory web-based training for all employees; 100% coverage of functions at risk; additional workshops/info sessions; induction training for new board and top management members includes ABC. ABC policies published internally; policy excerpt with guidelines available on the website.
- Metrics and outcomes:
  - Zero tolerance stance; effectiveness monitored by the Internal Control System.
  - 2024: no confirmed incidents of corruption or bribery and no related fines.
- Payment practices (G1-6):
  - Scope limited to invoices in Other administrative expenses and Other operating expenses; sampling used for some entities with a 90% confidence level due to data constraints.
  - Standard supplier payment terms followed by country (30 days in Germany, Austria, Bosnia & Herzegovina, Czech Republic, Croatia, Hungary, Romania; 60 days in Italy, Bulgaria, Serbia, Slovenia); average payment time of 19 days.
  - Expense mix: ICT services ~60% of relevant administrative expenses; marketing, consulting, and logistics ~22%; remaining ~18% individually not material (includes capitalized expenses and Other Operating Expenses).
  - No relevant pending legal proceedings related to late payments.
